source.title: CART: Context-Anchored Recurrent Transformer - A Parameter-Efficient Architecture with Learned Stability

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out perplexity across model widths and reports power-law fits, but also reports exponent softening and training-stage reversals that qualify the scaling picture. It does not use the original studies’ large-scale parameter/token/compute sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own width-scaling, training-stage, architecture-comparison, and downstream results. Related-work results cited from other papers, including their scaling laws, are not recorded as rows. The paper reports perplexity rather than held-out cross-entropy directly; the scaling evidence is therefore for perplexity, a transformed loss measure.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper on CART, a looped recurrent transformer, that also reports its own cross-width scaling results. It fits power laws to held-out perplexity across four widths at two training budgets, and evaluates zero-shot downstream tasks across the same widths. It is a new setting (small weight-shared recurrent model, at most about 1B tokens) with results on V1, V6 and V7. It runs no parameter, token or compute sweeps of the original kind, so it is not T1 or T2. It does not argue against any version, so it is not T5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase overweights scaling. The authors mainly conclude that CART does not deliver parameter efficiency at d=1024 and 1B tokens. Dense wins by 1–2% at stored-parameter parity and about 10% at effective-parameter parity. The gap splits into about 5% from weight sharing and about 5% from the architectural framing. Loop-count benefit seen at Stage 1 reverses at Stage 2, and the LTI gate settles at spectral radius 0.79–0.83. Width-scaling fits (exponent softening, possibly from under-training) and task-dependent downstream gains are secondary observations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a width sweep of a recurrent CART architecture and held-out perplexity, rather than the original papers’ large-scale parameter/token/compute scaling experiments or compute-optimal allocation procedure. It also reports downstream benchmarks and architecture comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Training budget changes the R-ranking: Stage 1 and Stage 2 show reversed per-scale predictions. The fitted width exponents differ between stages and soften across adjacent Stage 2 widths. Downstream trends vary by task. Stage 2 cross-scale CART comparisons use fixed token budget, while the paper notes that parameter/token ratios vary across widths.

fits_no_version.finding: Loop-count (R) rankings at fixed stored parameters reverse between 49M and 1B tokens. At Stage 1 the benefit grows with width; at Stage 2 R=6 is best for every d≥512.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rankings of architecture hyperparameters from short screening runs do not persist at longer training budgets.

record.problems: The Stage 2 sweep uses approximately 1B tokens per configuration, but the paper says the larger models are sub-Chinchilla and may not be near-converged. Cross-scale parameter-matched Dense baselines were not run; Dense comparisons are only at d=1024. The width power-law fits use four points. Downstream results are one seed per scale. The authors state that the apparent exponent softening could be sample variation or diminishing efficiency, and that further training is needed to distinguish explanations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. The paper's other results concern recurrent architecture mechanisms, throughput, spectral radius, or cited comparisons rather than the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No sweeps of parameters, tokens or compute with the other two non-limiting; no fits in loss; only about one order of magnitude in parameters.
No extrapolation of small-run fits to larger runs.
No sweep of depth, width or aspect ratio at fixed parameter count; only CART-versus-Dense comparisons at d=1024.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
No quantitative prediction of downstream scores from scale or loss; four tasks, one seed.
No variation of parameter counting, fitting method, data or schedule as such; no comparison of published laws.

missing.what: Cross-width perplexity on the FineWeb-Edu and TinyStories held-out sets at R=6 (PPLedu 41.52, 27.44, 23.15, 20.67). These are a second V1 curve with similar softening.

Unshared-core and self-attention-core CART versus Dense 12L at about 125M parameters: PPLwiki 19.22 and 19.27 versus 18.32 (4.9–5.2%, about 0.05 nats). Also CART R=1 versus Dense 7L at equal parameters: +2.2%. These are architecture differences at roughly fixed parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling results are incidental to an architecture paper. Perplexity power laws in width over a 4x range at a fixed token budget are a weak test of V1, because a power law in perplexity is not a power law in loss. The paper's parameter counts for d=1024 are internally inconsistent: Table 1 gives 125M stored and 179M effective, while the text uses 75M and 105M. Single author, preprint, AI-assisted drafting.

versions.untested_parts: Tests held-out perplexity across width for CART at the stated training budgets. Does not independently sweep parameters, tokens, or compute while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecking, nor establish the claim over several orders of magnitude.
No test of power-law fits from small runs predicting losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute search for the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation or fit of allocation trends against compute.
Only a d=1024 comparison of CART with Dense models at stored-parameter and effective-parameter parity; not a broad sweep of depth, width, or architecture details.
No power-law test in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests zero-shot downstream performance across four CART widths, not a quantitative prediction from pretraining loss or a broad range of downstream tasks.

Reports training-budget-dependent changes in recurrence rankings and width-fit exponents, plus possible cross-scale softening. Does not compare published law fits across studies or systematically vary parameter counting, fitting method, data, and training schedule.

rows.subject: CART (Stage 1 best-per-scale configurations)
rows.size_stated: d ∈ {256, 512, 768, 1024}; P=6; R=8 in the reported fit
rows.stage_stated: Stage 1, step 3,000
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to held-out Wikipedia perplexity across model widths
rows.measure: Held-out PPLwiki power-law fit against dmodel
rows.value: PPLstage1wiki(d) ≈ 2371 · d^-0.458; r² ≈ 0.999; each doubling of d reduces PPLwiki by approximately 28%
rows.note: Per the paper, the fit uses four points at (d, R=8, P=6) and step 3,000. This is a width/perplexity fit, not a direct loss fit over several orders of magnitude.
rows.check: The subject is not 'best-per-scale'. The text says the fit uses R=8 at every width, but Table 5 lists R=6 (184.9) as best at d=256. Table 11 also labels its Stage 1 column R=6 while showing the R=8 values. Stage 1 is only about 49M tokens (Section 5.2 says about 100M), and Figure 3 shows curves still falling, so tokens are the bottleneck. The fit is in perplexity against width, not loss against parameters, and covers only a 4x width range. It is an equally good fit, not a test of a loss power law.

source_check.correct: Section 7.3 specifies R=8, P=6 at all four widths. This is not best-per-scale: Table 5 selects R=6 at d=256. For V1, use cannot_determine: a four-point width/perplexity fit does not establish the specified loss law. Together with r2, the fitted exponent bears on V7 setup-dependence.
source_check.problem: The best-per-scale subject conflicts with the stated fixed-R fit; partial conflates an untested V1 law with V7 fit-dependence.

rows.measure: Held-out PPLwiki power-law fit against dmodel
rows.note: The paper describes the fit as four points and reports visible softening at the larger end.
rows.check: All widths use a fixed 1B tokens. Table 2 puts d=256 at 278% of Chinchilla-optimal and d=1024 at 28%, so the larger models are token-limited, outside V1's condition. The measure is perplexity, not loss. The authors note visible softening at the large end of the four-point fit.

source_check.correct: For V1, use cannot_determine: the fit measures perplexity against width at fixed approximately 1B tokens, with larger models explicitly token-limited. Together with r1, the differing fitted exponent supports V7 setup-dependence.
source_check.problem: The result does not demonstrate partial failure of V1 under its non-bottleneck condition.

rows.subject: CART P=6, R=6 versus Dense 7L
rows.size_stated: d=1024; Dense 7L is approximately 75M parameters and CART has approximately 75M stored parameters
rows.stage_stated: Stage 2, step 30,500; approximately 1B tokens; three-seed means
rows.operation_detail: Compare held-out Wikipedia perplexity at stored-parameter parity
rows.value: CART P=6, R=6: 20.35; Dense reported as better by 1.1%
rows.uncertainty: Dense standard deviation 0.06; CART standard deviation 0.08
rows.note: This is one parameter-matched architecture comparison, not a broad architecture-shape sweep.
rows.check: The paper's parameter counts conflict. Table 1 gives d=1024 CART 125.1M stored and 178.8M effective, yet Sections 4.3 and 7.1 call d=1024 CART about 75M stored and about 105M effective, which are the d=768 values. Parity is therefore uncertain. The 1.1% perplexity gap (about 0.01 nats) is small. This compares architecture families, not depth or width, so the link to V4 is loose.

rows.operation_detail: Compare held-out Wikipedia perplexity at effective-parameter parity
rows.uncertainty: Dense standard deviation 0.05; CART standard deviation 0.08
rows.note: The paper reports Dense as better; this is an architecture comparison at one width and training budget.
rows.check: 'Effective parameters' counts the shared core R times, so Dense 12L has more unique parameters than CART. The paper gives Dense 12L as about 105M in one place and about 125M in another. Because the models are not at matched parameter count in V4's sense, the 9.9% gap cannot challenge V4.
